newsitem.title: CANADA: Mitel shares tumble after Q4 warning.
newsitem.headline: Mitel shares tumble after Q4 warning.

text.p: Mitel Corp shares fell in Toronto and New York on Monday after the telecommunications equipment company said it would disappoint analysts with its fourth-quarter performance and take a charge.
Analysts said the news was bad but unsurprising. Industry observers are increasingly concerned that two of the three prongs of Mitel's business appear to be suffering.

Since many investors bought the stock because of prospects for its computer-telephony integration (CTI) products -- widely seen as one of the "hot" areas of telecommunications -- this augered ill for Mitel's share price, analysts said.
Mitel shares fell 1.15 to 8.70 on the Toronto Stock Exchange and 7/8 to 6-1/2 in New York.
The company said today it expected to take a C$13 million pre-tax restructuring charge in the fourth quarter of fiscal 1997 to cut operating expenses at its business communications systems unit.

Mitel expected its pre-charge fourth quarter results to be C$0.10 a share, below market expectations, because of continuing pricing pressures and higher operating costs on a global basis for the business communications business.
The stock was halted ahead of the announcement.
"There are going to be a lot of unhappy people out there," said one analyst who declined to be identified.

"I am not at all surprised to see this sort of thing today. I think Mitel's PBX business is a slow-growth business subject to price wars. CTI I don't think is working for Mitel and the semiconductor business is going well...but one out of three isn't enough," he added.
Duncan Stewart, money manager at Tera Capital, said a reasonable valuation for the stock would be in the C$6 to C$8 range, from 15 to 20 times forward earnings.
"We had already heard that Mitel's computer-telephony integration (CTI) products were taking longer than expected to be adopted," Stewart said.

"The news at the PBX (private branch exchange switching) level that at their low end, the systems are experiencing price pressure and at the high end, there are engineering problems with installation -- that's extremely bad news."

Stewart said the high-end private branch exchange systems were more difficult to install at customer sites than Mitel first intended, requiring the intervention of engineers that could add to cost and to set-up time.
